headline: Jodōshi is 助 (“to help”) plus 動詞 (“verb”), literally “helping verb”.

sources.quote: 助 (“to help”) + 動詞 (“verb”), literally “helping verb”

meaning: to bear in mind, to aim to do
headline: Kokorogakeru is 心 (kokoro, “attention, mind”) plus 掛ける (kakeru, “latch onto”).

sources.quote: From 心 (kokoro, “attention, mind”) + 掛ける (kakeru, “latch onto”).

headline: デコレーション is borrowed from English decoration.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English decoration.

headline: Daihon is from Sinitic 臺本 (táiběn).

sources.quote: From Sinitic 臺本／台本 (táiběn).

headline: Chōkan is 長 (chō, “chief, leader”) plus 官 (kan, “government official”), either a wasei kango or from Middle Chinese 長官.

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 長 (chō, “chief, leader”) + 官 (kan, “government official”). Either a wasei kango from these on'yomi readings, or from Middle Chinese 長官 (sum-of-parts reading: /ɖɨɐŋ kuɑn/).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Saikai is 再 (“re-”) plus 会 (“meeting”).

sources.quote: 再 (“re-”) + 会 (“meeting”)

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: In mahi, 麻 is a daiyōji replacing 痲.

sources.quote: 麻 is a daiyōji replacing 痲.

headline: Shinjō is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 情 (jō, “emotion”).

sources.quote: From 心 (shin, “heart”) + 情 (jō, “emotion”).

headline: Kaijū is 怪 (kai, “mysterious”) plus 獣 (jū, “beast”).

sources.quote: 怪(かい) (kai, “mysterious”) + 獣(じゅう) (jū, “beast”)
Comparable terms in other languages: Swedish vidunder, odjur

headline: Kokorobosoi is 心 (kokoro, “heart, feelings”) plus 細い (hosoi, “slender”), with hosoi voiced to bosoi by rendaku.

sources.quote: From 心 (kokoro, “heart, feelings”) + 細い (hosoi, “slender”).
The hosoi changes to bosoi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: メーカー is from English maker.

sources.quote: From English maker.

headline: Nozomashii is 望ま (nozoma), the irrealis of 望む (nozomu, “to wish, to hope, to want, to desire”), plus しい (-shī, adjective-forming suffix).

morphemes.meaning: to wish, to hope, to want, to desire

sources.quote: From 望(のぞ)ま (nozoma, 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb 望(のぞ)む (nozomu, “to wish, to hope, to want, to desire”)) + しい (-shī, adjective-forming suffix).

headline: ベース covers “base” and “bass”, and the source borrows both from English.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English base.
Borrowed from English bass.

headline: アクセル is a clipping of アクセラレータ (akuserarēta), from English accelerator.

sources.quote: Clipping of アクセラレータ (akuserarēta), from English accelerator.

headline: Ōsuji is 大 (ō-, “big”) plus 筋 (suji, “thread”).

sources.quote: 大(おお) (ō-, “big”) + 筋(すじ) (suji, “thread”)

headline: Ikigomu is 意気 (iki, “spirits, enthusiasm”) plus 込む (komu, “to go into; to be full of, to have a lot of”), with komu voiced to gomu by rendaku.

morphemes.meaning: to go into; to be full of, to have a lot of

sources.quote: Compound of 意気(いき) (iki, “spirits, enthusiasm”) + 込(こ)む (komu, “to go into; to be full of, to have a lot of”). The komu changes to gomu as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Gairyaku is likely from the Middle Chinese compound 概略, literally “generally, approximately + brief, abbreviated”.

sources.quote: Likely from Middle Chinese compound 概略 (gə̀i lɨɐk̚, literally “generally, approximately + brief, abbreviated”).

headline: Kyōtei is ultimately traceable to Middle Chinese 協定, but may be a recent Japanese term, attested only since 1877.

sources.quote: /keputei/ → /kefuteː/ → /keuteː/ → /kjoːteː/

Ultimately traceable back to Middle Chinese 協定 (MC hep dengH). However, this might be a much more recent term in Japanese, attested only since 1877, suggesting that this word may have been adopted as part of the modernization and internationalization efforts of the Meiji era (1868–1912).

headline: Jinsoku is from Middle Chinese 迅速 (MC swinH suwk).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 迅速 (MC swinH suwk).

headline: In kokuren, 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.

sources.quote: 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.

headline: Yūgure is 夕 (yū, “evening”) plus 暮れ (kure, “dusk, nightfall”), with kure voiced to gure by rendaku.

sources.quote: 夕(ゆう) (yū, “evening”) + 暮(く)れ (kure, “dusk, nightfall”).
The kure changes to gure as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to be used up, to be run out
headline: Tsukiru is from Old Japanese, found in the Man'yōshū and spelled phonetically as 都奇 and, in the Nihonshoki kayō, as 豆紀.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese tuki₂. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE, spelled phonetically in man'yōgana as 都奇, and in the Nihonshoki kayō (completed 720 CE) under the phonetic man'yōgana 豆紀.

meaning: to perform, to play (a part), to act
headline: Enjiru is a shift from the verb 演ずる (enzuru), as -uru verbs moved to the -iru pattern.

sources.quote: Shift from verb 演(えん)ずる (enzuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

headline: Kanazuchi is 金 (kana, “metal”) plus 槌 (tsuchi, “hammer, mallet”), with tsuchi voiced to zuchi by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 金 (kana, “metal”) + 槌 (tsuchi, “hammer, mallet”). The tsuchi changes to zuchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to set, to lay, to place
headline: Sueru is from the classical lower bigrade verb 据う (suu), and the source compares 座る (suwaru, “sit”).

sources.quote: From classical shimo nidan katsuyō verb 据う (suu), possibly parsed as *suwu. In the Muromachi period, there also exists a classical verb 据ゆ (suyu).
Compare 座る (suwaru, “sit”, intransitive).

headline: Haji goes back to Proto-Japonic.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *pantuy.

headline: Kō, “1st in rank”, is from Middle Chinese 甲.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 甲 (kæp).

headline: Danna is from Middle Chinese 旦那 and 檀那, both used as transliterations of a Sanskrit word for “generosity, giving, donating”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 旦那 (MC tanH na), 檀那 (MC dan na), both used as transliterations of Sanskrit दान (dā́na, “generosity, giving, donating”). Ultimately cognate with English donate and donor, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃nom.
Attested in Japanese sinophone sources since at least the 1000s and in vernacular Japanese sources since at least 1287.

sources.quote: Derived from Middle Chinese 封 (MC pjowng|pjowngH).

sources.quote: 教 (kyō, “to teach”) + 科 (ka, “section; department”)
